subject: VAPA
overview: Advanced Art & Portfolio runs 50 minutes a day as a studio course: fall builds drawing, painting, and media skills, and the year centers on a Sustained Investigation (modeled on AP 2-D Art and Design) that ends in a curated portfolio and a public senior exhibition. Your role is studio coach: show each technique or artist briefly, then give the student long working time, hold regular critiques (describe, analyze, interpret, evaluate), and keep them documenting their process and on pace (about 15 investigation pieces by spring). Grade with the rubrics given, and value experimentation and revision as well as polish.

weeks.prep: Gather a mixed-media sketchbook, graphite pencils 2H–6B, kneaded eraser, fineliners, a mirror, and a lamp. Download the College Board AP 2-D Art and Design course overview (portfolio = Sustained Investigation, 15 images, ~60% of score; Selected Works, 5 works, ~40%). Clear a studio corner with good light (a north-facing window or a daylight-balanced bulb).
misconceptions: Thinking the baseline portrait should be perfect. It's a record of where you start; honesty makes growth visible in June.
Believing talent matters more than practice. Skill grows through daily, deliberate practice; the sketchbook is the engine.
Treating the artist statement as an afterthought. Writing about intent clarifies the work throughout the year.

days.guide: Help the student organize supplies by type, set up lighting from one side to avoid glare, and photograph the space for the process journal.

questions.q: Why set up a consistent light source in a studio?
questions.a: Consistent, directional light makes values and color judgments reliable from session to session and reduces glare.

days.guide: Student draws a 45-minute mirror self-portrait. Remind them to block in the overall head shape first, then features; don't erase obsessively. Date and save it.

questions.q: Where are the eyes located on an adult head (front view)?
questions.a: About halfway between the top of the skull and the chin.

days.guide: Student fills two pages testing every medium (pencil grades, pen, marker, watercolor, etc.) and rates comfort 1–5.

questions.q: What's the difference between a 2H and a 6B pencil?
questions.a: 2H is harder and lighter (good for light guidelines); 6B is softer and darker (good for deep shadows).

days.guide: Review the AP portfolio structure together; student writes three specific goals.

questions.q: What are the two sections of the AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio?
questions.a: Sustained Investigation (15 images of works and process guided by an inquiry, with written responses) and Selected Works (5 works demonstrating skill and synthesis of materials, processes, and ideas).

days.guide: Student writes a half-page reflection on the artist they want to become.

questions.q: What is an artist statement?
questions.a: A short written explanation of an artist's ideas, intentions, and process that helps viewers understand the work.

weeks.assessment_key: Baseline self-portrait and goal sheet: proficient = complete 45-minute self-portrait from observation (dated), two-page media inventory with ratings, three specific measurable goals tied to the portfolio (e.g., 'complete 15 investigation pieces by March'), and a thoughtful reflection. 4 = goals include timeline and skills to build; 2 = vague goals or incomplete portrait; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Sketchbook, magazines, scissors, glue stick. Bookmark Smithsonian Learning Lab and the National Gallery of Art open-access images (NGA Images).
misconceptions: Choosing the first idea. Strong work usually comes from pushing past obvious ideas.
Thumbnails that are too detailed. Thumbnails are small, fast composition plans (value and placement), not finished drawings.
Using images found online as if they were free to copy. Use open-access or your own photos and cite sources.

days.guide: Student writes one word in the center and branches to 30 visual ideas (objects, places, memories, metaphors).

questions.q: Why use a mind map before drawing?
questions.a: It generates many associations quickly, helping move past obvious ideas to more personal, original ones.

days.guide: Student draws 20 two-inch thumbnails varying viewpoint, cropping, and value.

questions.q: What should a thumbnail sketch decide?
questions.a: Composition: placement of main shapes, viewpoint, cropping, and basic value pattern.

days.guide: Collect 10 references from open-access collections, noting source and credit line.

questions.q: What does 'open access' mean for museum images?
questions.a: The museum has released the images (often public domain) for free use, including reuse and adaptation.

days.guide: Make a quick magazine collage combining unexpected images into a new idea.

questions.q: How can collage help generate ideas?
questions.a: Juxtaposing unrelated images creates surprising combinations and new meanings.

days.guide: Present three strongest ideas to a family member; record feedback.

questions.q: What makes feedback useful?
questions.a: It is specific — what the viewer noticed, what they felt or understood, and questions it raised.

weeks.assessment_key: Sketchbook idea pages rubric. 4 – Mind map with 30+ ideas, 20 varied thumbnails, 10 credited references, collage, feedback recorded and three ideas developed with notes. 3 (proficient) – All components complete with variety. 2 – Missing components or repetitive thumbnails. 1 – Minimal.

weeks.prep: Choose an Art21 episode (art21.org, free; preview content). Sketchbook. Have a list of elements (line, shape, form, value, color, texture, space) and principles (balance, contrast, emphasis, movement, pattern, rhythm, unity/variety, proportion).
misconceptions: Formal analysis that jumps straight to opinions. Describe and analyze before interpreting or judging.
Copying an artist's style instead of learning from their process.
Thinking contemporary art must be 'pretty' to be good. It's judged by ideas and execution together.

days.guide: Watch the episode; note materials, process, ideas, and how the artist works in series.

questions.q: Define 'contemporary art.'
questions.a: Art made by living artists in the present era (roughly the late 20th century to today), often exploring current ideas and diverse media.

days.guide: Student writes a 300-word formal analysis: description, elements and principles, meaning.

questions.q: What is the difference between an element and a principle of art?
questions.a: Elements are the basic visual components (line, shape, color, value, texture, space, form); principles are how they're arranged (balance, contrast, emphasis, rhythm, unity, etc.).

days.guide: Study how the artist develops a series; student sketches three variations on one idea.

questions.q: What makes a group of works a 'series'?
questions.a: They share an idea, approach, or visual language while each explores a variation.

days.guide: Complete a small finished drawing inspired by the artist's process (not copying their look).

questions.q: How can you be influenced by an artist without copying?
questions.a: Borrow a process or way of thinking (e.g., working from found materials, repetition) and apply it to your own subject and style.

days.guide: Reflect on how the student's response changed after research.

questions.q: Why can research change how we see an artwork?
questions.a: Context — the artist's intent, history, and process — adds meaning that isn't visible at first glance.

weeks.assessment_key: Formal analysis rubric. 4 – Accurate description, analysis using at least four elements/principles with specific visual evidence, supported interpretation, and context from the video; 300 words. 3 (proficient) – Description, analysis, and interpretation with evidence. 2 – Mostly opinion or description only. 1 – Incomplete. Mini-work: proficient = completed drawing applying the artist's process to the student's own idea with a short note explaining the connection.

weeks.prep: White eggs (hard-boiled) or white objects, a single desk lamp in a darkened room, vine and compressed charcoal, toned paper, white charcoal or chalk, kneaded eraser, blending stump. Set up the still life before Day 3.
misconceptions: Outlining shadows with lines. Value is shown with tone; edges are where values meet.
Making reflected light as bright as the highlight. Reflected light is always darker than the lit side.
Keeping everything mid-gray. Push the darkest darks and preserve the white of the paper for highlights to create a full value range.

days.guide: Student makes a 10-step value scale in graphite and in charcoal, from white to black, with even steps.

questions.q: Why make a value scale?
questions.a: To practice control of pressure and layering and to have a reference for matching values across the full range.

days.guide: Draw eggs under one lamp; label highlight, light, halftone, core shadow, reflected light, cast shadow, and occlusion shadow.

questions.q: Where is the darkest part of the cast shadow?
questions.a: Right where the object touches the surface (the occlusion shadow).

questions.q: What is the core shadow?
questions.a: The darkest band on the object itself, where the form turns away from the light, just before reflected light.

days.guide: Set up a white still life with cups and fabric; begin a 3-hour chiaroscuro drawing — block in big shapes and shadow shapes first.

questions.q: What is chiaroscuro?
questions.a: Strong contrast of light and dark to model three-dimensional form (associated with Renaissance and Baroque artists like Leonardo and Caravaggio).

days.guide: Continue: push darkest darks, keep highlights clean, soften and sharpen edges deliberately.

questions.q: Why squint at a still life?
questions.a: Squinting simplifies detail and reveals the big value shapes and relationships.

days.guide: Finish; self-critique with a value checklist; photograph.

questions.q: Give one item for a value checklist.
questions.a: Full range from white to black; consistent light direction; reflected light darker than the lit side; cast shadows darkest near the object.

weeks.assessment_key: Chiaroscuro still-life rubric. 4 – Full value range, consistent single light source, convincing form with core shadow and reflected light, varied edges, accurate proportions, strong composition. 3 (proficient) – Clear light source, wide value range, believable form. 2 – Limited values or inconsistent light. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Ruler, drawing paper, fineliners; Drawabox.com lessons (free) for the 250-box challenge. Pick a room and a street/building view.
misconceptions: Placing vanishing points too close together in two-point perspective, which distorts boxes. Spread them wide, often off the page.
Horizon line confusion: it's always at the viewer's eye level.
Thinking atmospheric perspective is only about size. Distant objects also get lighter, cooler, lower in contrast, and less detailed.

days.guide: Draw 25 boxes in two-point perspective; check that parallel edges converge to the same vanishing point.

questions.q: In two-point perspective, what happens to vertical lines?
questions.a: They remain vertical (parallel); only the horizontal edges converge to the two vanishing points.

days.guide: Draw a room from life; mark eye level (horizon line) first.

questions.q: Where is the horizon line in perspective drawing?
questions.a: At the viewer's eye level.

days.guide: Draw your street or a building in three-point perspective (worm's-eye or bird's-eye).

questions.q: When is three-point perspective used?
questions.a: When looking steeply up or down at tall objects, so vertical lines also converge to a third vanishing point.

days.guide: Landscape study showing depth through value and detail changes.

questions.q: List three signs of atmospheric perspective.
questions.a: Distant objects appear lighter, bluer/cooler, lower in contrast, and less detailed.

days.guide: Select and refine the strongest piece.

questions.q: What is a vanishing point?
questions.a: A point on the horizon line where parallel lines appear to converge.

weeks.assessment_key: Perspective drawing rubric. 4 – Accurate horizon line and vanishing points, consistent convergence, convincing space, atmospheric effects or strong value structure, clean line quality, refined composition. 3 (proficient) – Mostly accurate perspective and convincing space. 2 – Inconsistent vanishing points. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: A willing family model (clothed) or a timed online pose site (e.g., Line of Action — check settings to exclude nudity), charcoal, newsprint pad, NGA open-access figure drawings by Michelangelo or Käthe Kollwitz.
misconceptions: Starting with outlines and details in gesture drawing. Gesture captures movement and the line of action in seconds.
Drawing heads too large. An adult figure is about 7.5–8 heads tall.
Avoiding hands. Simplify into mitten shapes and boxes before fingers.

days.guide: 30 one-minute gestures: find the line of action first, then rhythm of limbs.

questions.q: What is the 'line of action'?
questions.a: An imaginary curved line through the figure that captures its main movement or direction.

days.guide: Study head-unit proportions (≈7.5–8 heads tall; hips near the midpoint; elbows near the waist). Draw three 10-minute poses.

questions.q: About how many head-lengths tall is an adult figure?
questions.a: About 7.5 to 8 heads.

questions.q: Where does the halfway point of a standing adult fall?
questions.a: Around the hip/pubic bone.

days.guide: Fill a page with your hands and feet from multiple angles.

questions.q: What is foreshortening?
questions.a: The visual shortening of a form that points toward or away from the viewer.

days.guide: Copy a master figure drawing (e.g., Michelangelo's red chalk studies or Kollwitz's charcoal prints) to learn their mark-making.

questions.q: What can a master copy teach?
questions.a: How the artist simplified forms, used line and value, and built anatomy — by reconstructing their decisions.

days.guide: 45-minute figure drawing using gesture first, then proportion and form.

questions.q: Why start a long pose with a gesture?
questions.a: It establishes movement and overall proportion before details, keeping the figure alive and accurate.

weeks.assessment_key: Figure drawing set rubric. 4 – 30 lively gestures, accurate proportions in 10-minute poses, varied hand/foot studies with foreshortening, faithful master copy, 45-minute drawing with gesture, proportion, and form. 3 (proficient) – All components with generally accurate proportions. 2 – Stiff gestures or missing parts. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Charcoal, ink, brushes, mirror or photo references (own photos). Images of Alice Neel portraits and Kehinde Wiley portraits (e.g., his 2018 official portrait of Barack Obama). Print the four-step critique (describe, analyze, interpret, evaluate).
misconceptions: Thinking likeness is the only goal. Expressive portraits use distortion, color, and mark-making to convey personality and mood.
Placing features too high. The eyes sit at the halfway line; the nose bottom is about halfway between eyes and chin.
Critique as judgment only. Follow the four steps in order.

days.guide: Measured portrait: eyes at halfway; nose about halfway from eyes to chin; mouth about one-third from nose to chin; ears between brow and nose bottom; one eye-width between eyes.

questions.q: Where do the ears line up on a face in front view?
questions.a: Roughly between the brow line and the bottom of the nose.

days.guide: Study Neel (direct, psychologically intense portraits with blue outlines, expressive color) and Wiley (contemporary sitters in heroic Old Master poses against ornate patterned backgrounds).

questions.q: How does Kehinde Wiley challenge traditional portraiture?
questions.a: He paints contemporary Black sitters in the grand poses and settings of European portraits, questioning who has historically been shown as powerful.

days.guide: Create an expressive portrait conveying mood through marks and composition.

questions.q: Name two ways to convey mood in a portrait without changing the expression.
questions.a: Line quality (jagged vs. smooth), color/value key, cropping and composition, background treatment, lighting.

days.guide: Refine using a family member's feedback.

questions.q: What is 'likeness'?
questions.a: How recognizably the portrait resembles the specific person.

days.guide: Formal critique of the unit's drawings using describe, analyze, interpret, evaluate.

questions.q: List the four steps of formal critique in order.
questions.a: Describe, analyze, interpret, evaluate.

weeks.assessment_key: Expressive portrait rubric. 4 – Strong likeness or purposeful distortion, deliberate mark-making and composition conveying a clear mood, refined with feedback; critique notes complete all four steps with evidence. 3 (proficient) – Recognizable portrait with intentional expressive choices; critique uses four steps. 2 – Little expressive intent or incomplete critique. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Acrylic or gouache: a warm and cool version of each primary if possible (or one red, yellow, blue) plus white; for Day 4 a Zorn palette (yellow ochre, cadmium red light or vermilion, ivory black, titanium white). Brushes, palette, canvas paper, water containers.
misconceptions: Making colors darker with black only, which can dull them. Also use complements or darker hues.
Confusing value and saturation. Value is light/dark; saturation is intensity/purity.
Thinking a limited palette is limiting. It forces color harmony.

days.guide: Mix a 12-step wheel: 3 primaries, 3 secondaries, 6 tertiaries.

questions.q: What are the complementary pairs on the traditional (RYB) color wheel?
questions.a: Red–green, blue–orange, yellow–violet.

questions.q: Name the tertiary colors.
questions.a: Red-orange, yellow-orange, yellow-green, blue-green, blue-violet, red-violet.

days.guide: Paint a grayscale version then a full-color version of one object; compare values.

questions.q: Why paint in grayscale first?
questions.a: It separates value from hue so you can see whether the form reads; good value structure makes color work.

days.guide: Paint the same landscape warm-dominant and cool-dominant.

questions.q: How does color temperature affect space?
questions.a: Warm colors tend to advance; cool colors recede — useful for depth.

days.guide: Still life with a Zorn palette.

questions.q: What colors are in a Zorn palette, and how can you get a 'blue'?
questions.a: Yellow ochre, red (cadmium/vermilion), ivory black, white; black mixed with white reads as a cool blue-gray next to warm colors.

days.guide: Self-critique the studies.

questions.q: How do you lower saturation without changing value much?
questions.a: Mix in a small amount of the complement or a gray of the same value.

weeks.assessment_key: Color study sheets rubric. 4 – Accurate 12-step wheel with clean mixtures, grayscale/color pair with matching values, convincing warm vs. cool versions, harmonious Zorn still life, written self-critique applying terms (hue, value, saturation, temperature). 3 (proficient) – All studies complete and accurate. 2 – Muddy mixtures or missing studies. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Acrylic or oil paints (if oil, use odorless mineral spirits with ventilation or water-mixable oils), canvas or panel, brushes, palette knife. Set up a still life with strong light that stays the same all week (mark object positions with tape).
misconceptions: Starting with details. Work from large shapes to small, dark to light (in oils) or big masses first.
Overmixing on the canvas, leading to mud. Mix on the palette and place strokes deliberately.
Glazing in thick paint. Glazes are thin, transparent layers over dry paint.

days.guide: Tone the canvas with a mid-value wash (e.g., burnt sienna); block in a monochrome underpainting of shapes and shadows.

questions.q: Why tone the canvas first?
questions.a: It removes the intimidating white and gives a middle value so you can judge lights and darks more accurately.

days.guide: Block in large color shapes focusing on value relationships.

questions.q: What is a block-in?
questions.a: Laying in the large, simplified shapes of color and value before refining.

days.guide: Develop forms and edges; use glazing or impasto deliberately.

questions.q: Define glazing and impasto.
questions.a: Glazing: thin transparent layers over dry paint to modify color. Impasto: thick, textured paint application.

days.guide: Final details and highlights.

questions.q: Why save highlights for last?
questions.a: They're the lightest, most specific accents; placing them last keeps them clean and crisp.

days.guide: Reflect on process; photograph.

questions.q: What does 'fat over lean' mean in oil painting?
questions.a: Each upper layer should contain more oil (be more flexible) than the layer beneath it to prevent cracking.

weeks.assessment_key: Observational painting rubric. 4 – Accurate drawing and proportions, strong value structure, convincing color and light, intentional edges and paint handling (glazing/impasto), finished surface, reflective process writing. 3 (proficient) – Accurate values and color, finished painting, reflection. 2 – Weak value structure or unfinished. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Portable kit (small panels, limited palette, water, rags, a viewfinder), sun hat and water. Images of Granville Redmond's poppy fields and Guy Rose's coastal paintings (e.g., from the Irvine Museum or Laguna Art Museum) and works by Monet.
misconceptions: Trying to paint every detail outdoors. Plein air studies capture light and big shapes quickly before light changes.
Thinking California Impressionism simply copied the French. California painters adapted Impressionism to the intense light, landscapes, and color of California.
Interpretations without evidence from the painting.

days.guide: Compare California Impressionists (Redmond, a deaf painter known for poppy-covered hillsides; Rose, who lived near Monet at Giverny) with French Impressionists (Monet, Pissarro).

questions.q: What is plein air painting?
questions.a: Painting outdoors directly from the subject, capturing natural light and atmosphere.

questions.q: How did California Impressionism differ from French Impressionism?
questions.a: It focused on California's landscapes — golden hills, poppies, coast — with brighter, high-key light, and often painted wilder, less urban scenes.

days.guide: 1-hour morning study: thumbnail first, then big shapes and light.

questions.q: Why work quickly in plein air?
questions.a: Light and shadows change as the sun moves, so the effect lasts only about 1–2 hours.

days.guide: Paint the same scene in afternoon light; compare color and shadows.

questions.q: How does morning light differ from afternoon light?
questions.a: Morning light is often cooler and clearer; late afternoon light is warmer and more golden, with long shadows from the opposite direction.

days.guide: Begin a larger studio landscape from the studies.

questions.q: How should plein air studies be used in the studio?
questions.a: As references for true color and light, combined with photos for detail and a refined composition.

days.guide: Write two interpretations of a California landscape painting; defend one with visual evidence.

questions.q: What makes an interpretation defensible?
questions.a: It cites visible evidence (color, composition, subject, light) and context, rather than personal opinion alone.

weeks.assessment_key: Plein air studies and interpretation rubric. 4 – Two completed studies capturing distinct light conditions with accurate value and color temperature; written interpretations supported by specific visual evidence and context; one defended convincingly. 3 (proficient) – Two studies and two supported interpretations. 2 – Studies lack light contrast or interpretations unsupported. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Large paper or canvas, acrylics, palette knives, wide brushes; music for Day 2. Images: Kandinsky (Composition VII, 1913), Frankenthaler (Mountains and Sea, 1952), Rothko (color field paintings, 1950s).
misconceptions: Thinking abstraction is random. Strong abstraction uses deliberate composition, color, and contrast.
Believing abstract art has no meaning. Artists express emotion, music, or ideas through non-representational form.
Overworking an abstract piece until colors turn muddy.

days.guide: Compare Kandinsky (linked color and form to music; 'Concerning the Spiritual in Art,' 1911), Frankenthaler (soak-stain technique, thinned paint on raw canvas), Rothko (large soft-edged rectangles of color meant to evoke deep emotion).

questions.q: What technique did Helen Frankenthaler pioneer?
questions.a: Soak-stain: pouring thinned paint onto unprimed canvas so it soaks into the fibers.

questions.q: How did Kandinsky connect art and music?
questions.a: He believed colors and forms could act like musical tones and chords, evoking emotion without depicting objects.

days.guide: Four small abstract studies responding to a piece of music or an emotion.

questions.q: Name two visual choices that can express calm vs. anxiety.
questions.a: Calm: horizontal lines, cool harmonious colors, soft edges. Anxiety: jagged diagonals, clashing saturated colors, crowded composition.

days.guide: Begin a larger abstraction from the best study.

questions.q: What is color field painting?
questions.a: A style of Abstract Expressionism using large, flat areas of color to create an immersive, contemplative experience.

days.guide: Finish the abstraction and the Week 10 studio landscape.

questions.q: How do you know when an abstract painting is finished?
questions.a: When the composition feels resolved — balance, focal areas, and color relationships work — and further marks would weaken it.

days.guide: Painting critique (describe, analyze, interpret, evaluate); select one painting for the portfolio.

questions.q: What is Abstract Expressionism?
questions.a: A post-WWII American movement (New York School) emphasizing spontaneous, gestural, or color-field abstraction to express emotion.

weeks.assessment_key: Abstract painting and unit critique rubric. 4 – Abstraction shows clear intent (music/emotion), deliberate composition and color, developed from studies; critique uses all four steps with specific evidence; justified portfolio selection. 3 (proficient) – Intentional abstraction and complete critique. 2 – Little intention or partial critique. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Sketchbook; AP 2-D Art and Design sample Sustained Investigations and scoring guidelines (AP Central, free). Note the written prompts: identify the inquiry and describe how it guided the work; describe ways practice, experimentation, and revision guided the investigation.
misconceptions: Picking a theme instead of an inquiry. An inquiry is a question to explore ('How can I show memory fading using layered transparent media?'), not just a topic ('nature').
Planning 15 versions of the same picture. Each piece should push the question forward.
Choosing an inquiry for what judges might like rather than personal meaning.

days.guide: Review three AP sample Sustained Investigations and note how each inquiry guided the work and how pieces evolved.

questions.q: What is a Sustained Investigation?
questions.a: A body of work (15 images, including process) exploring a single inquiry through practice, experimentation, and revision.

days.guide: Brainstorm 10 inquiry questions from life, culture, or community.

questions.q: Turn the topic 'my grandmother's kitchen' into an inquiry question.
questions.a: Example: 'How can recipes, objects, and handwriting from my grandmother's kitchen be combined to show how family memory is passed down?'

days.guide: Narrow to one and write why it matters.

questions.q: What makes an inquiry strong?
questions.a: It is open-ended, personally meaningful, and visually explorable in many ways and materials.

days.guide: 15 thumbnails responding to the question.

questions.q: Why make many thumbnails before starting?
questions.a: To explore different visual approaches and avoid repeating the same idea.

days.guide: One-page proposal: inquiry, materials, artists to research, a 15-piece plan.

questions.q: What three things does the AP scoring emphasize in a Sustained Investigation?
questions.a: A clear inquiry; practice, experimentation, and revision; and synthesis of materials, processes, and ideas (with 2-D skills).

weeks.assessment_key: Sustained Investigation proposal rubric. 4 – Open-ended, personal inquiry question; explains significance; varied materials and processes; three relevant artists; 15-piece plan showing development (experimentation and revision); 15 thumbnails. 3 (proficient) – Clear inquiry, materials, artists, and plan. 2 – Topic rather than inquiry or thin plan. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Smithsonian Learning Lab and museum sites; sketchbook; materials for the first investigation piece. Discuss the difference between influence, homage, and appropriation.
misconceptions: Copying an artist's image into your portfolio. AP prohibits plagiarism; work must move beyond references.
Researching only famous Western artists. Look across cultures and contemporary artists.
Treating research as separate from making. Research should change your choices.

days.guide: Research three artists; build a reference page for each (images, process notes, connection to inquiry).

questions.q: What is the difference between influence and appropriation?
questions.a: Influence: learning from an artist's ideas or methods in your own work. Appropriation: deliberately borrowing existing images or objects and recontextualizing them.

days.guide: Process study imitating one artist's technique (not subject).

questions.q: What is an homage?
questions.a: A work that openly honors another artist, often referencing their style or a specific work.

days.guide: Research a related cultural tradition (e.g., Chicano muralism, Japanese woodblock prints).

questions.q: Name a feature of the Chicano mural movement.
questions.a: Large public murals (from the late 1960s–70s) celebrating Mexican-American identity, history, and political struggles, often made collaboratively with communities (e.g., Chicano Park, San Diego).

days.guide: Begin piece 1.

questions.q: Why start piece 1 even if it isn't perfect?
questions.a: Making reveals problems and ideas that planning can't; revision is part of the investigation.

days.guide: Process note: how research shaped piece 1.

questions.q: What belongs in a process note?
questions.a: What you tried, why, what you learned, and how it changes the next step.

weeks.assessment_key: Artist research pages rubric. 4 – Three artists with images (cited), process analysis, explicit connections to inquiry, cultural tradition research, process study, and a process note showing influence on piece 1. 3 (proficient) – Three cited artists with connections and a process note. 2 – Images without analysis. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: The student's chosen media; phone camera and even lighting for documentation. AP caption guidance: materials and processes, size; written responses are short (character limits).
misconceptions: Skipping documentation until the end. Photograph process (sketches, experiments) along the way; process images count.
Piece 2 repeating piece 1. Push the inquiry with a new material, viewpoint, or idea.
Vague feedback criteria.

days.guide: Complete piece 1.

questions.q: How do you know a piece is finished?
questions.a: It answers its part of the inquiry, the composition is resolved, and remaining changes wouldn't improve it.

days.guide: Photograph piece 1 and write a 100-character process caption.

questions.q: Write a sample 100-character caption.
questions.a: Example: 'Graphite and coffee wash on recipe cards; layered transfers to show fading memory.' (≈85 characters)

days.guide: Sketch three directions for piece 2.

questions.q: Name three ways to push an inquiry in a new piece.
questions.a: Change material/process, scale, viewpoint/composition, subject focus, or audience interaction.

days.guide: Begin piece 2 with a new material or composition.

questions.q: Why experiment early in an investigation?
questions.a: Experimentation reveals new possibilities and gives evidence of practice and revision.

days.guide: Mini-critique using skill, synthesis, and inquiry.

questions.q: What does 'synthesis' mean in AP Art scoring?
questions.a: How well materials, processes, and ideas work together to communicate the inquiry.

weeks.assessment_key: Pieces 1–2 progress rubric. 4 – Piece 1 complete and documented with a clear caption; piece 2 clearly extends the inquiry via new material or idea; process photos; feedback recorded with action steps. 3 (proficient) – Piece 1 done and documented; piece 2 underway with a new direction; feedback recorded. 2 – Undocumented or repetitive. 1 – Little progress.

weeks.prep: Chosen media; AP Sustained Investigation scoring guidelines (AP Central). Schedule a progress conference.
misconceptions: Scoring yourself generously without evidence. Point to visible proof for each row.
Avoiding revision of what didn't work. Revision is evidence of growth.
Losing track of the 15-piece timeline.

days.guide: Complete and document piece 2.

questions.q: What should process documentation show?
questions.a: Sketches, experiments, stages, and changes made — evidence of practice and revision.

days.guide: Begin piece 3, deliberately revising something that didn't work earlier.

questions.q: Give an example of purposeful revision.
questions.a: Changing from opaque paint to transparent layers because the first piece hid the handwriting the inquiry depends on.

days.guide: Continue piece 3.

questions.q: Why keep notes while working?
questions.a: They capture decisions for written responses and show how thinking evolved.

days.guide: Score the three pieces with the guidelines (inquiry; practice/experimentation/revision; materials, processes, ideas; 2-D skills).

questions.q: What evidence shows 'practice, experimentation, and revision'?
questions.a: Process images, varied approaches across pieces, and visible changes made in response to problems.

days.guide: Progress conference; update the plan.

questions.q: How many pieces should be finished at this point to stay on track for 15 by spring?
questions.a: About 3 (pieces 1–3), with pieces 4–5 planned before winter break.

weeks.assessment_key: Self-scored progress review: proficient = three pieces documented, each scored on all rubric rows with specific evidence, honest identification of weaknesses, and an updated timeline. 4 adds concrete revision strategies; 2 = scores without evidence; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Free software: Krita (painting), GIMP or Photopea (photo editing). Phone or tablet. Background on fair use (four factors) and cases: Rogers v. Koons (1992, Koons lost), Cariou v. Prince (2013, most of Prince's works found transformative), Andy Warhol Foundation v. Goldsmith (2023, Supreme Court ruled against the Warhol Foundation's licensing use). Creative Commons license types; CC0 public domain dedication.
misconceptions: Believing anything online is free to use. Most images are copyrighted by default.
Thinking changing an image 10% makes it legal. There is no such rule; fair use is a case-by-case four-factor analysis.
Assuming 'AI-generated' means no ethical questions. Training data, consent, and authorship are debated; AP rules require the work be the student's own.

days.guide: Teach copyright (automatic on creation), fair use (purpose/character, nature of work, amount used, market effect), Creative Commons. Analyze two appropriation cases.

questions.q: Name the four fair-use factors.
questions.a: 1) Purpose and character of the use (including transformative or commercial), 2) nature of the copyrighted work, 3) amount and substantiality used, 4) effect on the market for the original.

questions.q: Why did Jeff Koons lose Rogers v. Koons?
questions.a: He made sculptures closely copying Art Rogers's photograph 'Puppies' for commercial sale; the court found it wasn't fair use (it didn't parody the photo itself and harmed its market).

days.guide: Guided exercise in layers, masks, brushes.

questions.q: What is a layer mask?
questions.a: A grayscale mask on a layer that hides (black) or reveals (white) parts of the layer without deleting pixels — non-destructive editing.

questions.q: Raster vs. vector?
questions.a: Raster images are made of pixels (lose quality when enlarged); vector images use mathematical paths (scale without loss).

days.guide: Discuss AI image generation ethics; student writes a personal policy.

questions.q: Give one ethical concern about AI image generators.
questions.a: They may be trained on artists' work without consent or compensation; authorship and originality are unclear; they can imitate living artists' styles.

days.guide: Create a digital artwork using only own photos or CC0 sources.

questions.q: What does CC0 mean?
questions.a: The creator has waived copyright, placing the work in the public domain for any use without attribution required.

days.guide: Finish and document; cite sources.

questions.q: How should you cite a CC BY image?
questions.a: Give title, creator, source link, and license (e.g., 'Photo by X, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0').

weeks.assessment_key: Digital artwork and ethics statement rubric. 4 – Skilled use of layers/masks/brushes, connects to inquiry, all sources own or CC0 with citations; ethics statement explains copyright, fair use factors, and a thoughtful AI policy. 3 (proficient) – Complete digital work with correct sourcing and clear policy. 2 – Sourcing problems or thin policy. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Phone camera and a free editing app (Snapseed, Lightroom mobile). Plan shoots at golden hour (about the hour after sunrise / before sunset), midday, and by a window. Get permission before photographing people or private property.
misconceptions: Centering everything. Rule of thirds and leading lines create more dynamic compositions.
Heavy filters that hide weak photos. Edit for clarity and consistency.
Photographing people without consent.

days.guide: Shoot 50 photos practicing rule of thirds, leading lines, framing.

questions.q: What is the rule of thirds?
questions.a: Dividing the frame into a 3×3 grid and placing key subjects along the lines or at intersections for balance and interest.

days.guide: Shoot one subject in golden hour, midday, and window light; compare.

questions.q: Why is golden hour light popular?
questions.a: Low sun produces warm, soft, directional light with long shadows and less harsh contrast.

days.guide: Create a 6-image photo essay on community visual culture.

questions.q: What is visual culture?
questions.a: The images and visual objects in everyday life — signs, ads, murals, media — and how they shape meaning and identity.

days.guide: Edit and sequence the essay (opening image, variety of distance, closing image).

questions.q: How does aperture affect depth of field?
questions.a: A wider aperture (smaller f-number, e.g., f/2) gives shallow depth of field; a narrower aperture (e.g., f/16) keeps more in focus.

days.guide: Present with a statement on how images shape community life.

questions.q: What are the three parts of the exposure triangle?
questions.a: Aperture, shutter speed, ISO.

weeks.assessment_key: Photo essay rubric. 4 – Six strong, varied images with deliberate composition and light, coherent sequence, consistent editing, insightful statement on visual culture, ethical consent. 3 (proficient) – Six well-composed images in a logical sequence with a clear statement. 2 – Weak composition or sequencing. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gel medium (matte), laser prints or photocopies of own photos (inkjet doesn't transfer well), paper and wood scraps, brushes, sponge, found objects, paint. Space to lay out all semester work.
misconceptions: Using inkjet prints for gel transfers. Laser/toner prints transfer best.
Peeling paper before the gel dries. Let it dry fully (several hours or overnight) before rubbing off the paper.
Mixed media as random collage. Each material should carry meaning for the inquiry.

days.guide: Practice transfers: coat surface and print face with gel, press face-down, dry, dampen and rub off paper. Remember the image reverses.

questions.q: Why is a gel-medium transfer reversed?
questions.a: The print is placed face-down, so the image appears as a mirror image.

days.guide: Create a mixed-media work combining transfer, paint, and drawing.

questions.q: What is assemblage?
questions.a: Three-dimensional art made by combining found objects.

days.guide: Complete the piece.

questions.q: How can materials carry meaning?
questions.a: Their history and associations (e.g., old letters suggest memory) add content beyond the image.

days.guide: Lay out all work; select top 8.

questions.q: What criteria help select top pieces?
questions.a: Technical skill, strength of idea, connection to inquiry, and variety of approaches.

days.guide: Semester self-evaluation and presentation.

questions.q: What is the difference between collage and mixed media?
questions.a: Collage glues flat materials onto a surface; mixed media combines any different media (paint, drawing, collage, objects) in one work.

weeks.assessment_key: Semester portfolio review rubric. 4 – Top 8 selected with written justification, mixed-media piece integrates transfer/paint/drawing meaningfully, self-evaluation cites specific growth and goals, at least 5 investigation pieces documented. 3 (proficient) – Top 8 selected, self-evaluation with evidence, investigation on track. 2 – Selection without reasoning. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Sketchbook, investigation pieces so far, chosen media.
misconceptions: Thinking revising the inquiry means failure. Investigations evolve; AP asks how practice and revision guided the work.
Planning without material lists or time estimates.
Rushing pieces to hit numbers.

days.guide: Rewrite the inquiry based on discoveries.

questions.q: Why might an inquiry question change?
questions.a: Making reveals new directions or narrows the focus to what's most meaningful.

days.guide: Plan pieces 6–15 with thumbnails and a materials list.

questions.q: If 10 pieces remain and about 7 weeks are allotted for pieces, how fast must you work?
questions.a: About 1.5 pieces per week (10 ÷ 7 ≈ 1.4).

days.guide: Begin piece 6.

questions.q: What is a 'body of work'?
questions.a: A collection of related works developed around shared ideas or methods.

days.guide: Continue piece 6.

questions.q: What is a 'pivot' in an investigation?
questions.a: A purposeful change in direction based on discoveries.

days.guide: Finish and document piece 6.

questions.q: What information goes with each documented image?
questions.a: Title (optional), media/materials and processes, size (height × width × depth), date.

weeks.assessment_key: Updated plan and piece 6: proficient = revised inquiry with reason, thumbnails and materials for pieces 6–15 with timeline, piece 6 completed and documented with caption. 4 = clearly evolved inquiry; 2 = vague plan; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Very large paper or canvas and small cards for scale studies; chosen media.
misconceptions: Enlarging without changing approach. Scale changes mark-making, viewing distance, and impact.
Thinking small work is less important. Intimate scale draws viewers close.
Not documenting dimensions.

days.guide: Make a very small and a very large study of one idea.

questions.q: How does scale change a viewer's experience?
questions.a: Large works can overwhelm or immerse; small works invite close, intimate viewing.

days.guide: Begin piece 7 at a new scale.

questions.q: What does 'monumental' mean in art?
questions.a: Large in scale or impression, often commanding public space.

days.guide: Continue piece 7.

questions.q: Name a technical challenge of working large.
questions.a: Maintaining consistent proportions and value across the surface; need to step back often.

days.guide: Finish piece 7.

questions.q: What does 'intimate' scale mean?
questions.a: Small work meant to be viewed up close.

days.guide: Document and reflect on how scale changed meaning.

questions.q: Why include a scale reference when photographing?
questions.a: To show viewers the actual size, which affects interpretation.

weeks.assessment_key: Piece 7 and reflection: proficient = completed piece at a new scale, scale studies, documentation with dimensions, reflection explaining how scale changed meaning. 4 = scale clearly strengthens the inquiry; 2 = little reflection; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A material new to the student (beeswax with supervision, thread/embroidery, air-dry clay, coffee or tea staining). SAFETY: heat encaustic wax only with an adult, in a ventilated area, below smoking point.
misconceptions: Expecting a new material to work on the first try. Test first.
Using unusual media as a gimmick. Choose materials whose qualities support the idea.
Not recording experiments.

days.guide: Five sketchbook experiments with the new material; record results.

questions.q: Why test a new material before the final piece?
questions.a: To learn its behavior (drying time, layering, durability) and avoid ruining the final work.

days.guide: Begin piece 8 with the new material.

questions.q: Give an example of a material carrying meaning.
questions.a: Thread and stitching can suggest care, repair, or domestic labor.

days.guide: Continue piece 8.

questions.q: What is encaustic?
questions.a: Painting with heated, pigmented beeswax.

days.guide: Finish piece 8.

questions.q: What makes media 'unconventional'?
questions.a: Materials not traditionally used in fine art (coffee, thread, wax, found objects).

days.guide: Photograph and caption piece 8.

questions.q: How do you photograph textured work?
questions.a: Use raking (low-angle) side light to reveal texture, plus an evenly lit straight-on shot.

weeks.assessment_key: Piece 8 rubric. 4 – Five documented experiments, completed piece where the new material deepens the inquiry, skilled handling, clear caption. 3 (proficient) – Experiments and a completed piece connected to inquiry. 2 – Few experiments or weak connection. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: All investigation pieces; three viewers who haven't heard the student explain the work; recording sheet.
misconceptions: Explaining the work before viewers respond. Silent viewing tests whether the art communicates.
Dismissing unexpected readings. They can reveal strengths to build on.
Revising everything at once.

days.guide: Show pieces to three viewers without explanation; record interpretations.

questions.q: Why not explain the work first?
questions.a: To learn what the art communicates on its own.

days.guide: Compare interpretations with intent; decide which readings to strengthen.

questions.q: What is 'intent vs. reception'?
questions.a: The difference between what the artist means and what viewers actually perceive.

days.guide: Revise one earlier piece based on critique.

questions.q: Give an example of revision based on critique.
questions.a: Viewers missed the handwriting theme, so the student enlarged and darkened the text layer.

days.guide: Begin piece 9.

questions.q: How can critique shape the next piece?
questions.a: It reveals what's working to emphasize and what's unclear to address.

days.guide: Write a process reflection.

questions.q: What should the reflection include?
questions.a: Viewer responses, comparison with intent, decisions made, and evidence of revision.

weeks.assessment_key: Critique analysis rubric. 4 – Records three viewers' interpretations in detail, insightful comparison with intent, revised piece with before/after documentation, reflection guiding future work. 3 (proficient) – All responses recorded, comparison, one revision documented. 2 – Superficial. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Chosen media; research sources on the Chicano mural movement or Faith Ringgold (story quilts such as Tar Beach, 1988; American People Series of the 1960s).
misconceptions: Social art that preaches without visual strength. Message and form must work together.
Assuming art can't change beliefs. Movements like the Chicano murals changed public spaces and visibility.
Using another community's symbols without understanding.

days.guide: Complete piece 9.

questions.q: What does 'synthesis' mean for piece 9?
questions.a: Materials, processes, and ideas combining to express the inquiry clearly.

days.guide: Research an artist or movement that changed public beliefs; note strategies.

questions.q: What are Faith Ringgold's story quilts?
questions.a: Painted quilts combining images and handwritten narrative text, telling stories of African American life (e.g., Tar Beach, 1988).

questions.q: What strategies did Chicano muralists use?
questions.a: Large public murals in neighborhoods, community collaboration, imagery from Mexican and Indigenous history, addressing civil rights and identity.

days.guide: Begin piece 10 aimed at a social or community message.

questions.q: Name one strategy for a community message in art.
questions.a: Public placement, collaboration, recognizable symbols, text, or narrative.

days.guide: Continue piece 10.

questions.q: How do you avoid stereotypes in social-message art?
questions.a: Research, consult community members, and represent people with specificity and dignity.

days.guide: Finish and document pieces 9–10.

questions.q: Why document finished work immediately?
questions.a: To ensure high-quality images before work is moved, damaged, or altered.

weeks.assessment_key: Pieces 9–10 rubric. 4 – Both complete; piece 10 communicates a social message using strategies from research; strong technical execution; documented with captions. 3 (proficient) – Both complete and documented, piece 10 has a clear message. 2 – One incomplete. 1 – Little progress.

weeks.prep: Chosen media; a weekly studio schedule. Keep momentum.
misconceptions: Waiting for inspiration. Studio habits (regular time, warm-up sketches) keep work moving.
Abandoning pieces midway. Finish, then evaluate.
Documentation backlog.

days.guide: Begin and work on piece 11.

questions.q: Name two studio habits that build momentum.
questions.a: Working at a set time daily, starting with a warm-up sketch, leaving a piece at an easy re-entry point.

days.guide: Finish piece 11.

questions.q: What is 'momentum' in a body of work?
questions.a: Sustained productivity where each piece builds on the last.

days.guide: Begin piece 12.

questions.q: How should piece 12 differ from piece 11?
questions.a: It should extend the inquiry — a new angle, material, or composition — not repeat it.

days.guide: Continue piece 12.

questions.q: Why step back from your work frequently?
questions.a: To see the whole composition and values as a viewer will.

days.guide: Finish piece 12; document both.

questions.q: What is the AP Sustained Investigation image count?
questions.a: 15 images (which can include process images).

weeks.assessment_key: Pieces 11–12 rubric. 4 – Both completed with growing skill and clear development of inquiry, well documented with captions. 3 (proficient) – Both completed and documented. 2 – One incomplete. 1 – Little progress.

weeks.prep: All investigation pieces laid out; AP scoring guidelines; critique audience.
misconceptions: Calling it done without a gap analysis.
Adding filler pieces just to reach 15. Each piece should strengthen cohesion.
Scoring without the official rubric language.

days.guide: Lay out all pieces; identify gaps (missing experimentation, unresolved ideas, weak skills).

questions.q: What is 'cohesion' in a body of work?
questions.a: The pieces clearly relate through the inquiry while showing variety and development.

days.guide: Create or revise pieces to fill gaps.

questions.q: Give an example of a gap.
questions.a: No evidence of revision, or all pieces in one medium so experimentation isn't shown.

days.guide: Continue final pieces.

questions.q: How can process images help fill the 15?
questions.a: They show practice, experimentation, and revision, which AP explicitly scores.

days.guide: Finish the body of work (12–15 pieces).

questions.q: What written responses accompany the AP Sustained Investigation?
questions.a: Identify the inquiry and how it guided the work; describe how practice, experimentation, and revision guided it; for each image, materials, processes, and size.

days.guide: Full critique and AP-guideline scoring.

questions.q: What score range is AP Art and Design reported on?
questions.a: 1–5 (AP scale).

weeks.assessment_key: Completed Sustained Investigation rubric (aligned to AP rows). 4 – Clear inquiry guiding all work; strong evidence of practice, experimentation, and revision; materials, processes, and ideas synthesized; advanced 2-D skills; 15 documented images with concise written responses. 3 (proficient) – Inquiry evident, revision shown, good skill, 12–15 pieces documented. 2 – Weak connection or little revision. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Soft-cut linoleum or foam sheets, carving tools (V and U gouges) and a bench hook, water-based block ink, brayer, inking plate, spoon or baren, printing paper, pencil. SAFETY: always carve away from your body and keep the non-carving hand behind the blade. Images of Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa (c. 1831) and José Guadalupe Posada's calaveras.
misconceptions: Forgetting the image prints in reverse, especially text.
Carving toward the hand. Use a bench hook and carve away.
Inconsistent inking, which makes an uneven edition. Roll ink thinly and evenly.

days.guide: Study ukiyo-e (Edo-period Japanese woodblock prints, e.g., Hokusai and Hiroshige, multiple blocks for color) and Posada (Mexican printmaker whose calavera prints like La Calavera Catrina satirized society in cheap broadsides).

questions.q: How did printmaking spread ideas?
questions.a: Multiple copies could be made cheaply and distributed widely — Posada's broadsides reached ordinary people with news and satire.

questions.q: What is ukiyo-e?
questions.a: 'Pictures of the floating world' — Japanese woodblock prints (17th–19th centuries) of landscapes, actors, and daily life.

days.guide: Design the block; reverse the image (trace and flip).

questions.q: How do you prepare a design with text for a relief print?
questions.a: Draw or transfer it mirror-reversed onto the block so it prints correctly.

days.guide: Carve safely; pull test proofs.

questions.q: In relief printing, which areas print?
questions.a: The raised (uncarved) surfaces; carved-away areas stay the paper color.

days.guide: Print an edition of five with consistent registration.

questions.q: What is registration?
questions.a: Aligning the block and paper in the same position for each print (and for multiple colors).

days.guide: Sign and number prints in pencil: edition number (e.g., 3/5) lower left, title center, signature lower right.

questions.q: What does '3/5' on a print mean?
questions.a: It is the third print of an edition of five.

weeks.assessment_key: Print edition rubric. 4 – Five consistent prints with even inking and clean registration, design connects to inquiry, correct reversal, proper signing/numbering, safe carving. 3 (proficient) – Five prints mostly consistent, signed and numbered correctly. 2 – Inconsistent or unsigned. 1 – Fewer than three prints.

weeks.prep: Cardboard, wire, air-dry clay, found objects, hot glue (low-temp, supervise), paint. Images of Betye Saar's The Liberation of Aunt Jemima (1972) and Louise Nevelson's black wood wall assemblages.
misconceptions: Building without an armature, so pieces sag or collapse.
Designing only from the front. Sculpture in the round must work from all sides.
Found objects chosen only for looks; their history adds meaning.

days.guide: Study Saar (reclaimed a racist stereotype image, arming the Aunt Jemima figure to transform its meaning) and Nevelson (unified found wood scraps by painting them one color, usually black).

questions.q: How does Betye Saar's The Liberation of Aunt Jemima transform its found image?
questions.a: She placed a racist mammy figure holding a broom alongside a rifle and pistol with a raised Black Power fist, turning a stereotype into a symbol of resistance.

questions.q: Why did Louise Nevelson paint her assemblages a single color?
questions.a: To unify varied found wood pieces into one composition, emphasizing shape, shadow, and rhythm over the objects' original identities.

days.guide: Build a small maquette.

questions.q: What is a maquette?
questions.a: A small preliminary model of a sculpture.

days.guide: Build the sculpture with armature or assemblage.

questions.q: What is an armature?
questions.a: An internal support framework (wire, wood, foil) that holds the sculpture's form.

days.guide: Finish surfaces; paint or patina.

questions.q: What does 'in the round' mean?
questions.a: Sculpture meant to be viewed from all sides.

days.guide: Photograph from four angles.

questions.q: Why photograph sculpture from multiple angles?
questions.a: A single view can't show the full three-dimensional form.

weeks.assessment_key: Sculpture or assemblage rubric. 4 – Strong 3-D composition from all angles, stable construction, meaningful found objects or forms tied to inquiry, finished surfaces, four quality photos. 3 (proficient) – Stable, finished sculpture with clear intent and documentation. 2 – Unstable or unfinished. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Photos of a local site (park wall, library, underpass — public view, safe access), sketchbook, graph paper for a scaled rendering. Read about Judy Baca's The Great Wall of Los Angeles (begun 1976 in the Tujunga Wash flood-control channel; about 2,754 feet long; painted with hundreds of young people through SPARC; depicts California history from an ethnically diverse perspective).
misconceptions: Designing for yourself rather than the site's community.
Ignoring practical constraints (weather, maintenance, permits, budget).
Thinking public art is only murals. It includes sculpture, installation, and temporary works.

days.guide: Study The Great Wall of Los Angeles and its community process.

questions.q: What made The Great Wall of Los Angeles a community project?
questions.a: Judy Baca worked with hundreds of youth from diverse backgrounds and consulted historians and community members to depict histories often left out of textbooks.

days.guide: Photograph and analyze a site: audience, traffic, history, light.

questions.q: What does 'site-specific' mean?
questions.a: Art created for a particular location, responding to its physical, social, or historical context.

days.guide: Design a mural or installation with a scaled rendering (e.g., 1 inch = 2 feet).

questions.q: A wall is 30 ft × 10 ft. At 1 inch = 2 ft, how big is the rendering?
questions.a: 15 inches × 5 inches.

days.guide: Write a proposal with budget, materials, and community benefit.

questions.q: Name three budget items for a mural.
questions.a: Exterior paint and primer, anti-graffiti/UV clear coat, scaffolding or lifts, brushes/rollers, permits, insurance, artist fees.

days.guide: Present as if to a city arts commission.

questions.q: What do arts commissions usually look for?
questions.a: Artistic quality, community relevance and input, feasibility, safety, durability, and budget.

weeks.assessment_key: Public art proposal rubric. 4 – Site analysis with photos, scaled rendering, design responsive to community and history, realistic itemized budget and timeline, maintenance plan, persuasive presentation. 3 (proficient) – Site analysis, rendering, budget, community benefit, clear presentation. 2 – Missing budget or site response. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Phone or camera on a tripod (or stack of books), two identical lamps (same bulb type) at 45° or indirect window light, neutral gray/white backdrop, gray card or white paper for white balance, editing app.
misconceptions: Shooting at an angle, causing keystoning. Keep the camera centered and parallel to the artwork.
Using mixed light sources (lamp + window), which causes color casts.
Over-editing color so the photo no longer matches the work.

days.guide: Set up two lamps at 45° on either side, equal distance, neutral backdrop.

questions.q: Why place lights at 45° on both sides?
questions.a: It gives even illumination and reduces glare and hot spots.

days.guide: Photograph 2-D works square to the camera; correct glare (adjust angle/polarizer) and keystoning.

questions.q: What is keystoning?
questions.a: Distortion where a rectangle appears as a trapezoid because the camera isn't parallel to the artwork.

days.guide: Photograph 3-D works: multiple views plus a detail.

questions.q: What views should a 3-D work have?
questions.a: Front, side(s), back or three-quarter, and a detail.

days.guide: Crop, color-correct (white balance), export at 1200–2000 px on the long side.

questions.q: What does white balance correct?
questions.a: Color casts from the light source so whites appear neutral.

days.guide: Create an organized archive: title, media, dimensions (H × W × D), date.

questions.q: What order are dimensions listed in?
questions.a: Height × width × depth.

weeks.assessment_key: Digital archive rubric. 4 – All works photographed square, evenly lit, color-accurate, cropped, consistent sizes; 3-D works with multiple views; organized folders with complete metadata (title, media, H × W × D, year). 3 (proficient) – Accurate photos and complete metadata. 2 – Glare, keystoning, or missing info. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Digital archive, printed thumbnails. Check requirements of target colleges (many use SlideRoom; typically 10–20 pieces). Look up National Portfolio Day dates.
misconceptions: Including every piece. Curate: fewer strong works beat many uneven ones.
Ignoring each school's specific requirements.
Random sequencing. Open and close with strong pieces and create visual flow.

days.guide: Write selection criteria for a college portfolio and for an exhibition.

questions.q: How might criteria differ for college admission vs. an exhibition?
questions.a: College: show range of skills, observational drawing, and creative thinking. Exhibition: a cohesive theme and visual impact for the public.

days.guide: Select 15–20 for a college portfolio and 5 for AP-style Selected Works.

questions.q: What does AP Selected Works demonstrate?
questions.a: Five works showing skillful synthesis of materials, processes, and ideas.

days.guide: Sequence with printed thumbnails; justify order.

questions.q: Where should your strongest piece go?
questions.a: First (to make a strong impression), with another strong piece last.

days.guide: Get feedback from a teacher, artist, or National Portfolio Day reviewer.

questions.q: What is National Portfolio Day?
questions.a: Events where representatives from art colleges review prospective students' portfolios and give feedback.

days.guide: Revise selection.

questions.q: What is curation?
questions.a: Selecting and arranging works to communicate ideas and quality.

weeks.assessment_key: Curated portfolio selection rubric. 4 – Written criteria, 15–20 pieces showing range and quality, 5 Selected Works, thoughtful sequence with rationale, revisions documented from outside feedback. 3 (proficient) – Selection, sequence with justification, feedback applied. 2 – Uncurated. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Free portfolio site (Google Sites, Adobe Portfolio, Cargo). Final images and captions. Parental note: use a professional email and avoid posting home address or personal details.
misconceptions: Statements full of jargon ('juxtaposes liminal dichotomies'). Use clear, specific language.
Writing about technique only. Include ideas and why the work matters.
Publishing without testing on a phone.

days.guide: Draft a 200-word statement: inquiry, process, why it matters.

questions.q: What three things should an artist statement address?
questions.a: What you make (subject/media), how you make it (process), and why (ideas and meaning).

days.guide: Revise; remove jargon; read aloud.

questions.q: Why read a statement aloud?
questions.a: To catch awkward phrasing and ensure it sounds like you.

days.guide: Write captions: title, media, size, year, short note.

questions.q: Write a correct caption format.
questions.a: Example: Kitchen Memory, 2025. Graphite and gel transfer on wood, 18 × 24 in. — Note: recipe cards from my grandmother.

days.guide: Build site: gallery, statement, contact.

questions.q: What is a CV for an artist?
questions.a: A list of exhibitions, education, awards, and publications.

days.guide: Publish; test on phone and computer.

questions.q: Why test on mobile?
questions.a: Many viewers, including admissions readers, view portfolios on phones; layouts and image sizes must work.

weeks.assessment_key: Artist statement and published portfolio rubric. 4 – Clear, jargon-free 200-word statement addressing what/how/why; complete captions; site with organized gallery, statement, bio, safe contact info; tested on two devices. 3 (proficient) – Statement, captions, and functioning site. 2 – Unclear statement or missing captions. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Contact potential venues (library community room, co-op, café, church hall) early; floor plan of the venue; label paper; flyer software.
misconceptions: Waiting too long to book a venue.
Hanging work at random heights. Center artworks around 57–60 inches from the floor (museum standard).
Labels missing information.

days.guide: Secure venue and date.

questions.q: What questions should you ask a venue?
questions.a: Dates/hours, wall hanging methods allowed, lighting, insurance/liability, cost, setup times, accessibility.

days.guide: Choose an exhibition title and theme.

questions.q: Why does an exhibition title matter?
questions.a: It frames how visitors understand the work and draws interest.

days.guide: Draw an installation plan placing each work.

questions.q: At what height are artworks typically centered?
questions.a: About 57–60 inches from the floor to the center of the work.

days.guide: Write and print wall labels and an intro panel.

questions.q: What goes on a wall label?
questions.a: Artist name, title (italic), year, medium, dimensions, and optionally a short description or price.

days.guide: Design and send flyer/invitations.

questions.q: What must an invitation include?
questions.a: Title, artist, venue address, dates, opening reception time, and contact/RSVP info.

weeks.assessment_key: Exhibition plan rubric. 4 – Confirmed venue and date, meaningful title and theme statement, scaled installation plan with heights and spacing, complete labels and intro panel, professional flyer distributed. 3 (proficient) – Venue, plan, labels, flyer. 2 – Missing plan or labels. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Acid-free mat board (pre-cut mats are fine), mat cutter if available, acid-free hinging tape, frames, D-rings and hanging wire, screwdriver, level, pedestals or boxes painted white for 3-D work.
misconceptions: Using masking tape or regular tape on artwork. It yellows and damages paper; use acid-free hinging tape.
Hanging work in direct sunlight. UV light fades media.
Using sawtooth hangers on heavy frames. Use D-rings and wire.

days.guide: Research archival practices: acid- and lignin-free materials, UV-filtering glazing, stable humidity (~40–50%), avoid direct sun.

questions.q: Why use acid-free materials?
questions.a: Acidic paper and board yellow and become brittle over time, damaging the artwork they touch.

days.guide: Mat and/or frame 2-D works (hinge at the top with a T-hinge).

questions.q: How should artwork be attached to a mat?
questions.a: With acid-free hinges (e.g., T-hinges) at the top so the paper hangs freely and can expand/contract.

days.guide: Attach hanging hardware; prepare pedestals.

questions.q: Where should D-rings go on a frame?
questions.a: About one-quarter to one-third down from the top on each side, with wire strung between them.

days.guide: Mock hang at home; check spacing and sightlines.

questions.q: Why do a mock hang?
questions.a: To test spacing, order, and visual flow before installation day.

days.guide: Complete exhibition checklist and transport plan.

questions.q: How should framed work be transported?
questions.a: Wrapped with corner protectors and padding, glass taped or protected, stored upright and secured.

weeks.assessment_key: Prepared works rubric. 4 – All works matted/framed or mounted with archival materials, secure hardware, pedestals ready, mock hang photographed, complete checklist and transport plan. 3 (proficient) – Works prepared safely with hardware and checklist. 2 – Some works unprepared or non-archival methods. 1 – Not ready.

weeks.prep: Artwork, labels, level, measuring tape, hooks/nails, guest book, simple refreshments, lighting (clip lights if needed).
misconceptions: Installing without measuring, leading to uneven heights.
Artist talks that read the statement word for word.
Ignoring visitor feedback afterward.

days.guide: Install: measure, level, light, place labels.

questions.q: How do you hang a work centered at 58 inches?
questions.a: Measure 58 in. to the center, add half the frame height, subtract the distance from the hanging wire (pulled taut) to the frame top; place the nail there.

days.guide: Prepare a 5-minute artist talk: inquiry, process, highlights, what's next.

questions.q: What makes a good artist talk?
questions.a: A clear story of the inquiry, specific process moments, connection to viewers, and openness to questions.

days.guide: Host the opening; give the talk.

questions.q: What is a reception?
questions.a: A social event (often the opening) where visitors meet the artist and view the show.

days.guide: Review guest-book comments and conversations.

questions.q: Why review audience feedback?
questions.a: It shows how the work communicates to the public and informs future work.

days.guide: Deinstall carefully; write an exhibition report.

questions.q: What should an exhibition report include?
questions.a: Attendance, what went well, problems and solutions, feedback, photos, lessons for next time.

weeks.assessment_key: Exhibition and artist talk rubric. 4 – Professional installation (level, consistent heights, lighting, labels), engaging 5-minute talk, gracious hosting, thorough report with feedback analysis, careful deinstall. 3 (proficient) – Clean installation, clear talk, report. 2 – Installation issues or weak talk. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Baseline self-portrait from Week 1, mirror, same pencils and lighting. Arrange a mentor conversation (art teacher, local artist).
misconceptions: Growth analysis that only says 'I got better.' Cite specific visual evidence.
Judging only technique. Also assess ideas and process.
Comparing to others rather than to your past work.

days.guide: 45-minute self-portrait under similar conditions; compare with Week 1.

questions.q: Why use the same conditions?
questions.a: So differences reflect growth in skill, not changes in setup.

days.guide: Growth analysis with specific evidence.

questions.q: Give an example of specific evidence of growth.
questions.a: 'In September my shadows were outlined; now the core shadow and reflected light model the cheek.'

days.guide: Evaluate the investigation with technical and conceptual criteria.

questions.q: What is the difference between technical and conceptual criteria?
questions.a: Technical: skill with materials (drawing, value, color, craft). Conceptual: strength and development of ideas and meaning.

days.guide: Discuss the year with a mentor.

questions.q: What questions might you ask a mentor?
questions.a: What's the strongest work and why? What should I develop next? How did you build your practice?

days.guide: Final reflection on artistic identity.

questions.q: What is metacognition?
questions.a: Thinking about your own thinking and learning processes.

weeks.assessment_key: Growth analysis rubric. 4 – Side-by-side self-portraits, specific visual evidence of growth in at least four areas, evaluation through technical and conceptual lenses, mentor insights, thoughtful identity reflection. 3 (proficient) – Comparison with specific evidence and both lenses. 2 – General statements. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Internet access; local community college catalog; list of local open studios or life-drawing groups. Portfolio for the conference.
misconceptions: Thinking art careers mean only fine artist. Many paths use art skills (design, illustration, therapy, conservation, teaching).
Stopping art after high school without a plan.
Summer plans without goals or schedules.

days.guide: Research five careers and pathways.

questions.q: What training does an art therapist need?
questions.a: Typically a master's degree in art therapy plus supervised clinical hours and credentialing (e.g., ATR through the Art Therapy Credentials Board).

questions.q: What does a conservator do?
questions.a: Examines, preserves, and restores artworks using scientific and art-historical knowledge; usually requires a graduate degree.

days.guide: Find local open studios, life-drawing groups, or community-college classes.

questions.q: Why join a community art group?
questions.a: Regular practice, feedback, models/resources, and connection with other artists.

days.guide: Plan a summer project with goals and schedule.

questions.q: What makes a summer art plan realistic?
questions.a: Specific goals, weekly schedule, materials budget, and a finish date.

days.guide: Create a final sketchbook spread summarizing the year.

questions.q: What could a summary spread include?
questions.a: Key images, inquiry question, quotes from reflections, and goals.

days.guide: Portfolio conference: present final portfolio and plan.

questions.q: What is an artist residency?
questions.a: A program providing artists time, space, and sometimes funding to create work, often away from home.

weeks.assessment_key: Final portfolio conference rubric. 4 – Polished portfolio (online and physical), confident presentation of inquiry and growth, researched career/education plan, community resources, specific summer project. 3 (proficient) – Complete portfolio and clear plan. 2 – Incomplete materials or vague plan. 1 – Not prepared.
